tasks.short: Look up terms and rules in the classification manuals, judge which code fits, ask a senior coder or clinician when unsure, log the decision and check yearly code updates.

steps.what: Medical records specialist consults classification manuals to locate information about disease processes

loop.input: The coding question and the licensed classification, its index and the national coding guidelines; no patient data.
loop.output: The relevant manual sections and candidate codes, each with a citation.
loop.check: Code accepts only codes that exist in the current code table and links each to its section; the specialist reads the cited section.
loop.stop: One answer per question; no cited section means the specialist searches the manual.
loop.why_not_simpler: Questions are phrased in clinical language that a keyword index often misses.

steps.what: Medical records specialist judges which code fits the clinical picture
Medical records specialist asks a senior coder or the clinician when unsure
Medical records specialist writes the coding decision in the team's tips document
Medical records specialist checks yearly code updates against the team's tips

tasks.design: An answer desk over the licensed classification, its index, the national coding guidelines and the team's decision log ({DOCS}) returns the relevant sections and candidate codes with citations; the specialist reads each cited section and chooses. Decisions go into a structured decision log that the desk also searches, and a list of codes changed in the yearly update shows which tips need review. Judging the code and asking colleagues stay with people.
tasks.previous_blocker: Each question meant paging through the manual, index and old e-mails.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models can answer questions over licensed manuals and cite sections.
tasks.still_hard: The manual's licence must allow this use, and answers must be checked in the cited section.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing a consultant's shorthand means a different diagnosis than it seems.
tasks.altitude: The specialist reads cited sections instead of searching from scratch.

reach.learn: Whether a shared decision log cuts repeat questions.

evidence.claim: Language models can answer questions over a given set of manuals and cite the sections used.
Software used only to look up classification codes has no medical purpose and is not a medical device.

assumptions: Boundary: from a coding question to updated tips; coding the record is outside.
Input contract: licensed classification and guidelines from the national coding body; decision log kept by the coding team; fallback is the printed manual.
Judging and asking do not change.
No patient data go into the answer desk.
research_questions: How often does the cited section answer the question?

already_counted.description: Medical records specialist reads each cited section.

incremental.description: Medical records specialist reports wrong answers to the coding lead.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Transcribe dictated reports, look up unclear terms, ask the clinician about inaudible parts, format the report, get it signed, then file it and send copies.

steps.what: Medical records specialist listens to the dictation and transcribes the medical report

loop.input: The clinician's dictation audio and the hospital's medical word list.
loop.output: Report text in the dictated order, with unclear words marked.
loop.check: Code checks drug names and doses against the drug list and left or right against the order; the specialist corrects the text and the clinician signs.
loop.stop: One pass per dictation; poor audio goes to the specialist to type.
loop.why_not_simpler: Speech varies too much for fixed rules.

steps.what: Medical records specialist looks up unclear words, drug names and terms
Medical records specialist asks the clinician about inaudible passages
Medical records specialist formats the report in the department template
Clinician reviews and signs the report
Medical records specialist files the signed report in the patient record
Medical records specialist sends a copy of the report to the GP

tasks.design: Speech recognition trained on the hospital's medical word list turns dictations into report text, marks unclear words and checks drug names, doses and sides against the drug list and the order; the specialist corrects the text. The department template fills automatically, and once the clinician has signed in the record system ({OTHER}), the report is filed and sent to the GP by secure mail. Asking clinicians about inaudible parts stays with the specialist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Every dictation was typed from audio.
tasks.enabler_now: Medical speech recognition produces usable text from dictation.
tasks.still_hard: Accents, noise and new drug names cause errors that must be corrected.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing that 'fifteen' should be 'fifty' from the context of the dose.
tasks.altitude: The specialist corrects text instead of typing it.

reach.learn: Whether clinicians correct their own recognised text.

evidence.claim: Dutch GPs using an ambient scribe spent 42.7 seconds less on documentation per consultation, with consultation length unchanged.
Software with a medical purpose is a medical device under the MDR.
Health data are special category data under the GDPR.

assumptions: Boundary: from dictation to the report filed and sent; the clinical content is outside.

Input contract: dictations from clinicians; the order with side, drug and dose fields in its current version, entered by the requesting clinician in order entry; drug list from the hospital pharmacy; fallback is typing.
Clinicians' time is outside the specialist's savings.
research_questions: How many corrections per report remain?

already_counted.description: Medical records specialist corrects recognised text.

incremental.description: Medical records specialist keeps the medical word list current.
Clinicians correct more of their own text before signing.

approvals.approved_version: The report as signed by the clinician in s5; any change needs a new signature before sending.
The report as signed by the clinician in s5; a corrected report needs a new signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Poor audio and heavy accents keep more typing.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read referrals for urgency and appointment type, find a slot that fits the clinic's rules, agree the date with the patient, send the appointment letter and refill cancelled slots.

steps.what: Medical records specialist reads referrals for urgency and appointment type
Medical records specialist searches the clinic agenda for a slot that fits the rules
Patient agrees the appointment date on the phone
Medical records specialist phones patients to schedule medical appointments
Medical records specialist posts the appointment letter with preparation instructions
Medical records specialist refills cancelled and missed slots

tasks.design: The agenda in the record system ({OTHER}) proposes slots that fit the clinic's rules for urgency, appointment type and clinician, and non-urgent patients pick from the offered slots in the patient portal, so fewer calls are needed; the patient's own time moves from the call to choosing a slot online and is counted as customer time. Once the specialist has confirmed the agreed date, the letter with preparation instructions goes out through the portal. A waiting list shows who can take a cancelled slot. Reading referrals stays with the specialist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Slots were searched by hand and every appointment agreed by phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Record systems propose slots by rule, and patient portals offer self-booking.
tasks.still_hard: Frail and older patients often need a call.
tasks.human_edge: Fitting a worried patient in sooner when the referral sounds urgent.
tasks.altitude: The specialist confirms proposals instead of searching the agenda.

reach.learn: Whether waiting lists fill cancelled slots.

evidence.claim: Hospital record systems propose slots by rule and patient portals offer self-booking.
Health data are special category data; appointment letters must go through a secure channel.

assumptions: Boundary: from referral to refilled slots; the visit itself is outside.
Input contract: referrals from GPs through the referral system; slot rules set by the outpatient planner; fallback is phone and post.
Patient time is priced as customer time, not as the specialist's savings.
research_questions: Do no-shows fall with portal letters?

already_counted.description: Medical records specialist checks proposed slots.
Patients log in and choose a slot in the portal instead of agreeing it by phone.

incremental.description: Medical records specialist helps patients who cannot use the portal.
Patients read the preparation instructions in the portal and confirm.

approvals.approved_version: The appointment as agreed and confirmed by the specialist in s3; a changed date needs a new confirmation before the letter goes out.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Clinics with many frail patients save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The medical records specialist keeps coding judgement, clarifications and urgent planning; manual searches, typing dictations and phone rounds shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A specialist who spends time on the hard cases while routine text and slots arrive ready to check.
